screens.title: Abstract Classes and Methods
screens.narratorSegment: Abstraction lets us model only the essential behavior of an object while hiding implementation details we don't need right now. In Java that idea is realized largely through abstract classes and abstract methods. An abstract class acts as a blueprint: it can provide fields, constructors, and concrete helper methods, while declaring some methods as abstract so subclasses must implement them. This pattern is useful when many related classes share some code but also require class-specific behavior. For example, a generic Instrument can provide a name field and a tune method, while leaving play as an abstract action that each concrete instrument implements differently. Throughout this lesson you will see how to declare abstract classes and methods, the rules the compiler enforces, and common beginner mistakes like trying to instantiate an abstract class or forgetting to implement all abstract methods in a concrete subclass. We will also work a hands-on Employee activity to practice creating abstract classes, implementing required methods, and verifying outputs. By the end you should be able to decide when an abstract class fits your design and how to implement it safely.

screens.title: What is Abstraction?
screens.narratorSegment: Abstraction is the practice of exposing only what is necessary about an object and hiding the rest. In object-oriented design this helps us reduce complexity and communicate intent: we define what an object can do without forcing every user to know how it does it. A concrete analogy is driving a car: the driver needs the steering wheel and pedals, not the engine plumbing. In Java we express abstraction with abstract classes and abstract methods. An abstract class can collect shared state and helper methods that are common to many subclasses, while abstract methods name behaviors that each subclass must implement. For example, an abstract Shape might specify area and perimeter as conceptual behaviors; each concrete shape supplies its own calculation. A common misconception is that abstraction equals lack of code: abstract classes can and should include concrete methods where it reduces duplication, such as a shared tune method for instruments. Another confusion is thinking abstraction only hides data; instead, abstraction defines a contract — a set of required behaviors. Reflect on a system you know: what essential behaviors would you expose as abstract methods, and which details would you hide inside concrete helpers?

keyIdea.title: Abstraction defined
keyIdea.text: Expose essential behavior; hide implementation. Use abstract types to express that contract in Java.

content.html:
Core Concept Abstraction
Abstraction
Separate what something does from how it does it.
Definition & key idea

Abstraction exposes essential behaviors as contracts. Use abstract classes to group shared fields and helpers, and declare abstract methods for the behaviors that vary.

Analogy: Driving a car
Driver uses steering and pedals; engine details are hidden.
Misconception
Abstract doesn't mean empty: abstract classes can contain concrete methods and fields to reduce duplication.
Key Takeaway

Abstraction defines a contract: name the behavior you require, allow subclasses to provide the how.

Practical mapping
When designing a class hierarchy, ask: which behaviors must every subtype implement? Make those abstract methods. Put shared code into the abstract parent to avoid duplication.
Example: Instrument
All instruments can be tuned and have a name; how they play differs and is therefore abstract.
Check your understanding
Name one class in your codebase that could become abstract because it shares helpers but requires different specific behavior across subclasses.

screens.title: Abstract Class Syntax and Rules
screens.narratorSegment: An abstract class in Java is declared with the abstract keyword before class. This single keyword tells the compiler the class may contain incomplete method declarations and therefore cannot be instantiated. The class may still include fields, constructors, and concrete methods. A core rule: if a class contains at least one abstract method, the class itself must be declared abstract. Another rule affects subclasses: any concrete subclass that inherits abstract methods must provide implementations for all of them. If it does not, that subclass must also be declared abstract. These rules enforce a contract across the hierarchy. A common beginner error is attempting to create an object of the abstract parent using new — the compiler rejects that because the parent is incomplete. Another error is writing an abstract method with a method body; abstract methods must end with a semicolon and have no body. Keep these rules in mind while you design: they guide the structure of your classes and the place where concrete behavior must live. Try writing a simple abstract class now and deliberately omit an implementation in a subclass to observe the compiler's helpful message.

keyIdea.title: Syntax rules
keyIdea.text: Declare abstract methods without bodies; classes with abstract methods must be declared abstract and cannot be instantiated.

content.html:
Definition Abstract Class Syntax
Rules at a glance
  • If a class has an abstract method, it must be declared abstract.
  • Abstract methods have no body and end with a semicolon.
  • Abstract classes can have constructors, fields, and concrete methods.
  • Concrete subclasses must implement all inherited abstract methods or be declared abstract.
Common mistake
Trying to instantiate an abstract class with new will cause a compilation error.
Quick syntax example
<!-- Java example shown for structure -->
abstract class Animal {
  String name;

  public Animal(String name) {
    this.name = name;
  }

  public abstract void makeSound();

  public void sleep() {
    System.out.println(name + " is sleeping.");
  }
}
Note: abstract methods have no body and end with a semicolon.

screens.title: Instrument Example: Abstract class with concrete helpers
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided Instrument example to see abstract classes in action. The Instrument class is declared abstract and contains a name field and a constructor to initialize it. It declares play as an abstract method — no body — which forces subclasses to implement it. At the same time, Instrument defines tune and getName as concrete methods that every subclass can reuse. Guitar and Piano extend Instrument, provide constructors that call super, and override play with their specific behavior. When you create Guitar and Piano objects and call tune and play, each subclass runs its own play implementation while reusing tune. This example also shows a common pattern: use the abstract parent for shared data and helpers, and leave behavior that varies to subclasses. A misconception learners often have is thinking the abstract parent can't have a constructor; it can, and that's useful to enforce initial state. If you try to new Instrument directly the compiler will complain. As a mental check, imagine adding a default play in Instrument — doing so would remove the abstract requirement, but also remove the enforced implementation from subclasses. Ask yourself: which methods should be required versus optional in your own designs?

keyIdea.title: Instrument pattern
keyIdea.text: Abstract parent holds shared state and helpers; concrete subclasses implement required behavior.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough Instrument Example
Instrument: abstract parent and subclasses
See how abstract and concrete members work together.
Code
// Abstract class Instrument
abstract class Instrument {
  String name;

  public Instrument(String name) {
    this.name = name;
  }

  // Abstract method: subclasses MUST implement this
  public abstract void play();

  // Concrete method: subclasses inherit this implementation
  public void tune() {
    System.out.println(name + " is being tuned.");
  }

  public String getName() {
    return name;
  }
}

class Guitar extends Instrument {
  public Guitar(String name) {
    super(name);
  }

  @Override
  public void play() {
    System.out.println(getName() + " is strumming a melody.");
  }
}

class Piano extends Instrument {
  public Piano(String name) {
    super(name);
  }

  @Override
  public void play() {
    System.out.println(getName() + " is playing a chord progression.");
  }
}
What to observe
  • Instrument defines play but does not implement it.
  • Guitar and Piano each provide play implementations.
  • Concrete methods tune and getName are reused by subclasses.
Example run
Creating new Guitar("Stratocaster") and calling tune() then play() prints subclass-specific output while reuse tune.
Key Takeaway

Use abstract classes to enforce required behavior while sharing implementation through concrete helpers.

screens.title: Subclass Implementation Rules
screens.narratorSegment: When a class extends an abstract class the compiler enforces a clear process. Step one: the subclass inherits fields and concrete methods from the parent. Step two: for every abstract method declared in the parent, the subclass must either provide a concrete override or itself be declared abstract. If you provide overrides, they must match the method signature and return type. Step three: once a subclass has provided concrete implementations for all inherited abstract methods it can be instantiated with new. A common beginner mistake is forgetting one abstract method — the compiler will raise an error explaining that the subclass is not abstract and does not override the abstract method. Another frequent confusion is expecting the parent to provide a default implementation; if the parent contains an abstract method, it deliberately has no body so subclasses are forced to decide the behavior. This process helps ensure certain behaviors always exist on concrete instances. As you design hierarchies, plan which behaviors are mandatory and which can be supplied by the parent as helpers to minimize duplicated code in subclasses. Subclass Implementation Rules means concrete subclasses must implement all inherited abstract methods or be abstract themselves; then they can be instantiated.. In practical terms, what happens when you extend an abstract class. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Subclass contract
keyIdea.text: Concrete subclasses must implement all inherited abstract methods or be abstract themselves; then they can be instantiated.

content.html:
Process Flow Subclass Implementation
Subclass Implementation Rules
A short, enforced process that ensures required behavior exists on instances.
Steps
  1. Inherit parent fields and concrete methods.
  2. Implement every abstract method or declare the subclass abstract.
  3. Once concrete, the subclass can be instantiated.
  4. Override signatures must match the parent's abstract method signatures.
Misconception
Declaring a subclass abstract to avoid implementing methods is valid, but delays when and where concrete behavior is defined.
Example error scenario
If Vehicle has public abstract void start() and Car extends Vehicle without implementing start(), then attempting to compile Car causes an error: Car is not abstract and does not override start(). The fix is to implement start() or declare Car abstract.
Pro tip
Use IDE quick-fixes to add stub implementations when you extend an abstract class; the stubs remind you where behavior is required.

keyIdea.text: Use an abstract parent to require a method, then provide different implementations for each subclass's behavior.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Employee Example
Employee: template and completed solution
Implement calculateAnnualBonus differently per subclass.
Completed code
abstract class Employee {
  String name;
  double monthlySalary;

  public Employee(String name, double monthlySalary) {
    this.name = name;
    this.monthlySalary = monthlySalary;
  }

  public void displayInfo() {
    System.out.println("Employee: " + name + ", Monthly Salary: $" + monthlySalary);
  }

  // Abstract method to be implemented by subclasses
  public abstract double calculateAnnualBonus();
}

class SalariedEmployee extends Employee {
  public SalariedEmployee(String name, double monthlySalary) {
    super(name, monthlySalary);
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateAnnualBonus() {
    // 10% of annual salary
    return monthlySalary * 12 * 0.10;
  }
}

class HourlyEmployee extends Employee {
  int hoursWorkedPerMonth;

  public HourlyEmployee(String name, double monthlySalary, int hoursWorkedPerMonth) {
    super(name, monthlySalary);
    this.hoursWorkedPerMonth = hoursWorkedPerMonth;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateAnnualBonus() {
    double bonus = 500.0;
    if (hoursWorkedPerMonth > 160) {
      bonus += (hoursWorkedPerMonth - 160) * 10;
    }
    return bonus;
  }
}

public class CompanyPayroll {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    SalariedEmployee alice = new SalariedEmployee("Alice Smith", 5000.0);
    HourlyEmployee bob = new HourlyEmployee("Bob Johnson", 2000.0, 180);

    alice.displayInfo();
    System.out.println("Alice's Annual Bonus: $" + alice.calculateAnnualBonus());

    bob.displayInfo();
    System.out.println("Bob's Annual Bonus: $" + bob.calculateAnnualBonus());
  }
}
What to check
  • calculateAnnualBonus returns a double in each subclass.
  • SalariedEmployee uses monthlySalary * 12 * 0.10.
  • HourlyEmployee applies base and overtime correctly.
Key Takeaway

Use abstract methods to create required variations and concrete methods to share helpers across subclasses.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Compiler Messages
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners commonly run into two compiler-led issues when working with abstract classes. The first is attempting to instantiate an abstract class directly. The language disallows this because the abstract class may contain incomplete behavior and therefore cannot produce a runnable instance. The compiler will report that you cannot instantiate the type. The fix is to instantiate a concrete subclass instead. The second frequent issue is extending an abstract class without implementing all of its abstract methods. The compiler states that your subclass is not abstract and does not override the abstract method, reminding you either to add the missing override or declare the subclass abstract. Another mistake is placing a method body inside an abstract method; abstract methods must contain only a signature and end with a semicolon. When you read these compiler messages, treat them as guidance: they indicate whether you left required behavior undefined. A practical debugging approach is to review the parent class for abstract signatures, then add stubs in the subclass and fill them with behavior. This stepwise fix helps you understand the contract the abstract parent imposes.

keyIdea.title: Fixing errors
keyIdea.text: Compiler messages describe missing implementations or illegal instantiation; follow them to add overrides or use concrete subclasses.

content.html:
Comparison Errors vs fixes
Common Mistakes and Fixes
Read compiler messages carefully; they point to missing contract fulfillment.
Error: Cannot instantiate abstract class
Cause: Using new with an abstract class. Fix: instantiate a concrete subclass or make the type concrete by implementing all abstract methods.
Example
Instrument inst = new Instrument("X"); — invalid. Use new Guitar("X") instead.
Error: does not override abstract method
Cause: Subclass did not implement an abstract method. Fix: add @Override method with matching signature or mark subclass abstract.
Debug tip
Use IDE quick-fixes to auto-generate method stubs, then implement behavior and remove TODOs.
Why it matters

These errors enforce correct design: they prevent creating incomplete objects and make required behavior explicit in concrete types.

screens.title: Designing with Abstract Classes
screens.narratorSegment: Abstract classes are a design choice for when you want to supply shared implementation and also require certain methods be provided by subclasses. Use them when multiple related types share fields and helper methods but have distinct core behaviors. For instance, if several animal types share hydration and sleep helpers but each makes a different sound, an abstract Animal with a concrete sleep method and an abstract makeSound method fits well. Structurally, place reusable fields and protected helper methods in the abstract parent to minimize duplication. Keep abstract methods focused and few; too many abstract methods can make the parent effectively empty and reduce its usefulness. A helpful pattern is to provide template methods: a concrete method in the parent that calls abstract hooks implemented by subclasses. This allows the parent to control sequence while subclasses supply specifics. A common design mistake is overusing abstract classes when composition or small helper classes would be simpler. Always ask whether shared behavior truly belongs in the parent or whether a utility class or delegated component makes the design clearer. screens.title: Class Hierarchy: 'Is-a' Relationship with Abstract Parents
screens.narratorSegment: Abstract classes participate in standard inheritance and express an is-a relationship: if Guitar extends Instrument then a Guitar is an Instrument. That relationship matters at both design and runtime: code that expects an Instrument can operate on any concrete subclass, relying on shared behavior and the guaranteed abstract contract. For example, a method playInConcert(Instrument i) can call tune and play without knowing the concrete type. The abstract parent ensures play exists on concrete subclasses. A frequent misunderstanding is thinking inheritance only copies code; it also defines type relationships that enable polymorphism. Another point is constructors: an abstract class can have constructors used by subclasses via super to enforce initialization. When designing the hierarchy, keep parent responsibilities narrow and avoid deep chains of abstract classes unless each level adds meaningful constraints. Think about what a caller needs to rely on: those required behaviors belong in the abstract parent so callers can program to the abstract type rather than concrete subclasses. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three concise ideas in mind. First, abstraction means exposing essential behavior while hiding implementation details; use it to reduce complexity and communicate intent. Second, an abstract class is a blueprint that can include fields, constructors, and concrete helper methods while declaring abstract methods that have no body and force subclass implementation. Third, an abstract method is a required contract: concrete subclasses must implement every inherited abstract method, or be declared abstract themselves. These rules are enforced by the compiler and prevent creating incomplete objects. Together these concepts let you design class hierarchies where common code is shared and specific behavior is safely delegated to subclasses. After this chapter, you should be able to design a narrow abstract contract and implement concrete types that fulfill it.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Three concise reminders to carry forward: First, never instantiate an abstract class; it's a template for subclasses. Second, abstract methods declare required behavior without an implementation; concrete subclasses must provide those implementations. Third, abstract classes may include concrete methods, constructors, and fields — use them to share common code and initialization. These rules enforce a contract that makes your code safer and more extensible. When designing, identify the smallest useful contract to place in the abstract parent, keep helper logic concrete, and let subclasses implement the specifics. The hands-on Employee and Instrument examples are practical ways to exercise these ideas and help you read and act on compiler messages when things go wrong. Ask yourself after each change: does this parent define the behavior clients need to rely on? If yes, it belongs in the abstract class; if not, consider moving it elsewhere.

fullNarratorScript:
Abstraction lets us model only the essential behavior of an object while hiding implementation details we don't need right now. In Java that idea is realized largely through abstract classes and abstract methods. An abstract class acts as a blueprint: it can provide fields, constructors, and concrete helper methods, while declaring some methods as abstract so subclasses must implement them. This pattern is useful when many related classes share some code but also require class-specific behavior. For example, a generic Instrument can provide a name field and a tune method, while leaving play as an abstract action that each concrete instrument implements differently. Throughout this lesson you will see how to declare abstract classes and methods, the rules the compiler enforces, and common beginner mistakes like trying to instantiate an abstract class or forgetting to implement all abstract methods in a concrete subclass. We will also work a hands-on Employee activity to practice creating abstract classes, implementing required methods, and verifying outputs. By the end you should be able to decide when an abstract class fits your design and how to implement it safely.

By the end of this pair of objective screens you will be able to define abstraction in object-oriented design, distinguish abstract and concrete classes and methods, implement abstract classes to enforce common behavior across a class hierarchy, and explain the limitations and compiler rules tied to abstract types. Each objective connects to a practical skill: defining the abstract contract, writing the Java syntax correctly, providing concrete implementations in subclasses, and debugging common compilation errors. For example, you will understand why an abstract class cannot be instantiated and why a concrete subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods. That knowledge lets you design hierarchies where shared code lives in the abstract parent while concrete behavior lives in subclasses like Guitar and Piano. During practice you'll also use constructors and concrete helper methods inside abstract classes to reduce duplication. Keep these objectives in mind as checkpoints: they guide which examples you write and which errors you fix. After you implement the Employee exercise, check each objective to confirm you can name, write, and reason about the abstract constructs you used.

These objectives map directly to exercises and checks you will complete. First, after defining abstraction you'll write brief notes explaining the essential behavior you want to expose — for instance, what does play mean for an Instrument? Second, to distinguish concrete from abstract, you'll declare an abstract class and then try instantiating it to observe the compiler's error. Third, implementation practice asks you to extend the abstract parent and provide concrete method bodies for every abstract method. The Employee hands-on activity exercises exactly that workflow: write an abstract Employee with a calculateAnnualBonus abstract method, then create SalariedEmployee and HourlyEmployee subclasses that implement it correctly and show outputs. Finally, for rules and limits you'll intentionally produce and then fix common mistakes such as forgetting an override, leaving an abstract method unimplemented, or using new with an abstract type. Each practice step ends with a quick reflection: can you explain why the compiler required the change? That reflection ensures you have not only written code but understood the enforcement behind abstract classes.

Abstraction is the practice of exposing only what is necessary about an object and hiding the rest. In object-oriented design this helps us reduce complexity and communicate intent: we define what an object can do without forcing every user to know how it does it. A concrete analogy is driving a car: the driver needs the steering wheel and pedals, not the engine plumbing. In Java we express abstraction with abstract classes and abstract methods. An abstract class can collect shared state and helper methods that are common to many subclasses, while abstract methods name behaviors that each subclass must implement. For example, an abstract Shape might specify area and perimeter as conceptual behaviors; each concrete shape supplies its own calculation. A common misconception is that abstraction equals lack of code: abstract classes can and should include concrete methods where it reduces duplication, such as a shared tune method for instruments. Another confusion is thinking abstraction only hides data; instead, abstraction defines a contract — a set of required behaviors. Reflect on a system you know: what essential behaviors would you expose as abstract methods, and which details would you hide inside concrete helpers?

An abstract class in Java is declared with the abstract keyword before class. This single keyword tells the compiler the class may contain incomplete method declarations and therefore cannot be instantiated. The class may still include fields, constructors, and concrete methods. A core rule: if a class contains at least one abstract method, the class itself must be declared abstract. Another rule affects subclasses: any concrete subclass that inherits abstract methods must provide implementations for all of them. If it does not, that subclass must also be declared abstract. These rules enforce a contract across the hierarchy. A common beginner error is attempting to create an object of the abstract parent using new — the compiler rejects that because the parent is incomplete. Another error is writing an abstract method with a method body; abstract methods must end with a semicolon and have no body. Keep these rules in mind while you design: they guide the structure of your classes and the place where concrete behavior must live. Try writing a simple abstract class now and deliberately omit an implementation in a subclass to observe the compiler's helpful message.

Let's walk through the provided Instrument example to see abstract classes in action. The Instrument class is declared abstract and contains a name field and a constructor to initialize it. It declares play as an abstract method — no body — which forces subclasses to implement it. At the same time, Instrument defines tune and getName as concrete methods that every subclass can reuse. Guitar and Piano extend Instrument, provide constructors that call super, and override play with their specific behavior. When you create Guitar and Piano objects and call tune and play, each subclass runs its own play implementation while reusing tune. This example also shows a common pattern: use the abstract parent for shared data and helpers, and leave behavior that varies to subclasses. A misconception learners often have is thinking the abstract parent can't have a constructor; it can, and that's useful to enforce initial state. If you try to new Instrument directly the compiler will complain. As a mental check, imagine adding a default play in Instrument — doing so would remove the abstract requirement, but also remove the enforced implementation from subclasses. Ask yourself: which methods should be required versus optional in your own designs?

When a class extends an abstract class the compiler enforces a clear process. Step one: the subclass inherits fields and concrete methods from the parent. Step two: for every abstract method declared in the parent, the subclass must either provide a concrete override or itself be declared abstract. If you provide overrides, they must match the method signature and return type. Step three: once a subclass has provided concrete implementations for all inherited abstract methods it can be instantiated with new. A common beginner mistake is forgetting one abstract method — the compiler will raise an error explaining that the subclass is not abstract and does not override the abstract method. Another frequent confusion is expecting the parent to provide a default implementation; if the parent contains an abstract method, it deliberately has no body so subclasses are forced to decide the behavior. This process helps ensure certain behaviors always exist on concrete instances. As you design hierarchies, plan which behaviors are mandatory and which can be supplied by the parent as helpers to minimize duplicated code in subclasses.
